rows.selection_reason: With no prior experiments, the most informative first step is to establish a minimal baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest RNA configuration with the most standard encoder, providing a clear performance anchor. This baseline will allow subsequent experiments to isolate the effect of (a) richer RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt), (b) multiprofile aggregation (avgpool vs. transformer), (c) adding the image modality (image_only or multimodal), and (d) fusion strategy. Starting from the simplest, lowest-risk configuration avoids confounding multiple design choices at once and gives a reference point against which every added complexity can be evaluated, making it the most efficient use of the first experiment under a limited budget.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), giving a minimal baseline. The most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries useful signal for this task at all. Question: config_010 (image-only, single-profile, ResNet-50) provides a clean, single-variable contrast to config_001—same profile setting (singleprofile), no aggregation or fusion—so the comparison isolates the effect of modality. Why this is the best next experiment: In a multimodal study, knowing the relative strength of each modality in isolation is the foundational decision that shapes every subsequent choice (which encoder to prioritize, whether fusion is worthwhile, whether multiprofile aggregation is needed). If image-only performs comparably or better than RNA-only, it justifies investing budget in multimodal fusion configurations; if it is much weaker, it redirects attention toward improving the RNA side (better encoders, multiprofile). This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty with a single clean comparison, avoiding the confound of simultaneously introducing a new modality, a new fusion strategy, and a new profile setting.

Evidence: With only two completed experiments, RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% acc while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak at 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the PCA representation is near-optimal or whether a learned biological encoder (scVI) can substantially improve RNA signal quality. This experiment (config_004: RNA, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001, changing only the RNA encoder while holding modality and profile setting constant. It directly tests whether a learned, lower-dimensional (200-d) representation can match or exceed a high-dimensional (2000-d) linear one. This is the best next step because the answer determines whether to invest remaining budget in scvi/scgpt-based configurations or to focus on aggregation and fusion strategies with PCA; it reduces uncertainty about a fundamental representation choice that gates many downstream decisions.

Evidence: scvi_n200 (config_004, acc=0.520) is our best RNA encoder, clearly outperforming pca_n2000 (config_001, acc=0.485). Image alone (config_010, acc=0.208) is very weak, so the RNA modality is the primary driver. Uncertainty: We have no data on whether multiprofile aggregation adds value over singleprofile for the best encoder. This is a fundamental design axis that will determine the strategy for all downstream multimodal experiments. Question: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) directly extends our best singleprofile result by adding multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool), isolating whether multiple profiles carry complementary signal. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a minimal, clean change from our strongest configuration (only profile_setting and the required aggregation differ), it tests a design decision that propagates to every multimodal config, and using avgpool (rather than transformer) keeps the experiment simple so we can attribute any change to the multiprofile representation itself. If multiprofile helps, subsequent experiments should prioritize multiprofile multimodal configs; if not, we can focus budget on singleprofile multimodal or better image encoders.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved 0.6501 acc, a large +0.13 jump over its singleprofile counterpart config_004 (0.5203), making multiprofile+scvi the strongest direction so far. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the simple avgpool aggregation is sufficient or whether a transformer aggregator can further exploit the multi-profile structure. This experiment (config_006) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding encoder (scvi_n200) and profile setting (multiprofile) fixed, giving a clean isolated comparison against config_005. This is the best next experiment because it directly exploits the strongest evidence (the multiprofile+scvi direction) while resolving a critical design choice—aggregation strategy—that will govern all subsequent multimodal and multiprofile experiments. If transformer substantially outperforms avgpool, it signals that the multiprofile benefit is underexploited and justifies more complex aggregation; if they are comparable, avgpool is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward encoder or fusion questions.

Evidence: The largest gain so far comes from switching to multiprofile with scvi_n200 (0.520 → 0.650, +0.13), while avgpool and transformer aggregation are nearly equivalent (~0.65). We also know scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000 in the singleprofile setting (0.520 vs 0.485). Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the multiprofile benefit is encoder-agnostic or specific to scvi_n200's learned latent space. This experiment (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) directly isolates the RNA encoder effect while holding profile setting and aggregation constant, enabling a clean comparison against config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool). If pca_n2000 also benefits substantially from multiprofile, the profile setting is the dominant driver and we can broaden our search; if not, the scvi_n200 + multiprofile interaction is critical and we should prioritize that encoder for further exploration (e.g., scgpt or multimodal fusion). This single-variable test is the most informative next step before committing budget to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (0.48-0.65 vs image 0.21), multi-profile with scVI is the current best (0.650-0.653), and scVI clearly outperforms PCA in both single and multi-profile settings. The aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) appears negligible (0.650 vs 0.653). Key uncertainty: whether scGPT, the third available RNA encoder, can improve on scVI in the multi-profile setting where the largest gains have been observed. This experiment (config_008: scGPT, multi-profile, avgpool) is a clean A/B comparison against config_005 (scVI, multi-profile, avgpool = 0.650), isolating the encoder effect while holding profile setting and aggregation constant. Under a limited budget, resolving which RNA representation is best in the highest-performing regime is the most informative next step before investing in multimodal or aggregation variants, since RNA is clearly the dominant signal source.

Evidence: The best RNA-only configuration (config_006: scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) achieves 0.653 acc, while image-only (resnet50) is very weak at 0.208. The critical unresolved question is whether the image modality provides any complementary signal when fused with the strong RNA representation, or whether it merely adds noise. This experiment (config_032: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is a minimal extension of our best RNA-only result—adding only the image branch and a simple concat fusion—so it cleanly isolates the effect of multimodal fusion. If it matches or exceeds 0.653, multimodal exploration is justified and we can then test ViT, weighted fusion, or other extensions. If it underperforms, we save budget by ruling out the entire multimodal branch. It is the highest-information experiment because the answer determines the direction of all subsequent experiments, and it changes only one design axis (adding image+fusion) relative to the known best configuration.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_032 (scvi_n200 + resnet50, multiprofile, transformer, concat) at 0.688 acc, but image-only resnet50 performs very poorly (0.208 acc), raising uncertainty about whether the image modality is contributing meaningful signal or just noise that happens to complement RNA. Question: config_038 isolates the image encoder choice by swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l while holding all other settings identical to config_032 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer, concat). This directly tests whether a stronger, pretrained vision transformer yields a meaningfully better image representation that improves multimodal fusion. Why this is the best next experiment: The image encoder is a fundamental design axis with high uncertainty—resnet50's poor standalone performance suggests it may be capping the multimodal ceiling. If ViT-L substantially improves over resnet50, it reshapes the entire multimodal design space and justifies further investment in the image modality; if it does not, we can conclude the image contribution is limited and focus budget on RNA-side refinements or fusion strategy. This single-variable comparison is maximally informative per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_038: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) achieves 0.721 accuracy, clearly outperforming the RNA-only best (0.653) and the resnet50 multimodal (0.688). This confirms that scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + multiprofile is the strongest design combination. However, all multimodal experiments so far have used concat fusion; weighted fusion has never been tested. Question: config_039 changes only the fusion method (concat → weighted) while holding every other design choice identical to config_038, cleanly isolating the effect of fusion strategy. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a single-variable, high-information experiment that directly tests whether a more expressive fusion mechanism can further improve on the current best. If weighted fusion helps, we gain a concrete performance improvement; if it does not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect budget toward other unexplored axes (e.g., image-only ablation or scgpt in multimodal). Under a limited budget, exploiting the strongest known direction with a minimal, well-isolated change is more efficient than a broader exploratory jump.
